chapter.title: Design a Unique ID Generator in Distributed Systems
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Design a distributed unique-ID generator that produces numeric, 64-bit, time-ordered IDs at more than 10,000 IDs per second, while comparing multi-master replication, UUIDs, ticket servers, and a Twitter Snowflake-like design.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 7 explains why a traditional database auto_increment primary key is insufficient for large distributed systems: one database server is not enough, and coordinating unique IDs across multiple databases with minimal delay is difficult. The chapter first clarifies the requirements—IDs must be unique, numeric, fit in 64 bits, increase with time, and support more than 10,000 IDs per second. It then compares four approaches: multi-master replication, UUIDs, a centralized ticket server, and a Twitter Snowflake-like generator. The first three each violate one or more requirements. Snowflake divides a 64-bit ID into a sign bit, 41-bit timestamp, 5-bit datacenter ID, 5-bit machine ID, and 12-bit sequence number. The deep dive explains why timestamps make IDs sortable, how the 41-bit timestamp lasts about 69 years, and how the 12-bit sequence permits up to 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine. The wrap-up highlights clock synchronization, section-length tuning, and high availability.
why_auto_increment_is_not_enough: A single database server is not large enough for the target distributed environment.
Generating unique IDs across multiple databases with minimal delay is challenging.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain why a single auto_increment database is not sufficient for distributed ID generation.
State all five requirements for the ID generator.
Explain multi-master replication and why its IDs increment by k rather than 1.

Explain how the timestamp field makes generated IDs sortable by time.
Explain the role and operational safety requirements of datacenter ID and machine ID.
Explain the 12-bit sequence field and its per-millisecond generation capacity.

Explain why using a recent custom epoch postpones timestamp overflow.
Discuss clock synchronization, section-length tuning, and high availability as follow-up topics.

requirements.detail: Every generated ID must be unique.
IDs do not have to increase by exactly 1, but IDs created later in time should be larger than IDs created earlier in time.
Generate over 10,000 unique IDs per second.

clarification_dialogue.candidate_question: What are the characteristics of unique IDs?
clarification_dialogue.interviewer_answer: IDs must be unique and sortable.

clarification_dialogue.candidate_question: For each new record, does ID increment by 1?
clarification_dialogue.interviewer_answer: The ID increases with time, but not necessarily by exactly 1. IDs created in the evening are larger than IDs created in the morning on the same day.

clarification_dialogue.candidate_question: Do IDs only contain numerical values?
What is the ID length requirement?
What is the scale of the system?

candidate_solutions.name: Multi-Master Replication
candidate_solutions.mechanism: Use each database server's auto_increment feature, but increment IDs by k instead of 1, where k is the number of database servers.
advantages: ID generation capacity can scale with the number of database servers.
disadvantages: Hard to scale across multiple data centers.
IDs do not increase with time across multiple servers.
Does not scale well when a server is added or removed.

candidate_solutions.name: UUID
candidate_solutions.mechanism: Each web server independently generates UUIDs without coordinating with other servers.
candidate_solutions.source_probability_statement: The chapter quotes a reference saying that even generating 1 billion UUIDs per second for about 100 years would only then bring duplicate probability to 50%.
candidate_solutions.source_wording_note: The chapter text uses the word 'collusion' in this sentence; this guide preserves the source's substantive claim without silently rewriting the chapter's terminology elsewhere.
advantages: No synchronization issue between ID generators.
Easy to scale because each web server can generate the IDs it consumes.
disadvantages: UUIDs are 128 bits, while the requirement is 64 bits.
UUIDs do not increase with time.

candidate_solutions.name: Ticket Server
candidate_solutions.mechanism: Use a centralized database server with auto_increment to issue unique numeric IDs.
candidate_solutions.chapter_reference: Flickr developed ticket servers for distributed primary keys.
advantages: Works for small- to medium-scale applications.
disadvantages: A single ticket server is a single point of failure.
Using multiple ticket servers to avoid the single point of failure introduces synchronization challenges.
candidate_solutions.meets_requirements: Not selected for the target distributed design

candidate_solutions.name: Twitter Snowflake-like Generator
candidate_solutions.mechanism: Divide one 64-bit ID into multiple sections so uniqueness, time ordering, distributed generation, and high throughput can be achieved without one centralized auto_increment database.

solution_comparison.key_issue: Single point of failure; multiple ticket servers introduce synchronization problems
Clock synchronization and careful section/ID assignment

fields.purpose: Reserved for future uses; the chapter notes it could potentially distinguish signed and unsigned numbers.

fields.meaning: Milliseconds since an epoch or custom epoch.
fields.purpose: Makes IDs sortable by time because the timestamp increases over time.

fields.behavior: Increment for every ID generated by the same machine/process within a millisecond; reset to 0 every millisecond.

snowflake_deep_dive.configuration_warning: Datacenter IDs and machine IDs are generally selected at startup and fixed while the system is running. Accidental changes can create ID conflicts.

timestamp_deep_dive.importance: The chapter calls the timestamp the most important 41 bits.
timestamp_deep_dive.sortability: As the timestamp increases with time, the generated IDs are sortable by time.
timestamp_deep_dive.custom_epoch_benefit: Choosing a custom epoch close to the current date delays the point at which the 41-bit timestamp overflows.
timestamp_deep_dive.after_exhaustion: After roughly 69 years, use a new epoch or adopt another migration technique for IDs.

sequence_deep_dive.normal_behavior: The field is 0 unless more than one ID is generated in the same millisecond on the same server.

capacity_derivations_from_source.note: The following arithmetic is derived directly from the bit allocations in the chapter. These combined capacities are study calculations, not additional claims printed by the source.
capacity_derivations_from_source.requirement_comparison: The required throughput is over 10,000 IDs/second, far below the theoretical sequence capacity of one machine if every millisecond were fully utilized.

wrap_up_topics.problem: The design assumes ID-generation servers share the same clock, but this assumption may fail across cores and machines.
wrap_up_topics.chapter_reference_solution: Network Time Protocol (NTP) is described as the most popular solution.
wrap_up_topics.implementation_detail_scope: Detailed clock-synchronization solutions are outside the scope of the book.

wrap_up_topics.idea: The bit allocation can be changed for workload needs. The chapter gives fewer sequence bits and more timestamp bits as an example for low-concurrency, long-term applications.
The ID generator is mission-critical and therefore must be highly available.

key_concepts.definition: A system that generates unique identifiers across multiple machines without relying on a single traditional auto_increment database.
An ID whose ordering reflects creation time; later IDs are larger than earlier IDs under the chapter's requirement.
Multiple database servers generate IDs using auto_increment with a step size equal to the number of servers.
A 128-bit identifier that can be generated independently by different servers with extremely low duplicate probability.
A centralized database server using auto_increment to issue numeric IDs.
A 64-bit ID assembled from timestamp, location/machine identity, and sequence fields.
The reference time from which the timestamp field measures elapsed milliseconds.
A chosen reference timestamp, typically near the system's start time, which extends the useful life of a fixed-width timestamp field.
The 5-bit Snowflake field identifying one of up to 32 datacenters.
The 5-bit Snowflake field identifying one of up to 32 machines in a datacenter.
The 12-bit per-machine counter used to distinguish IDs generated in the same millisecond.
The requirement that distributed ID generators have compatible notions of time so timestamp-based ordering does not break.

flashcards.front: What problem does Chapter 7 ask you to design?
flashcards.back: A unique ID generator for distributed systems.

flashcards.front: Why not simply use a traditional auto_increment primary key?
flashcards.back: One database server is not large enough for the distributed target, and coordinating unique IDs across multiple databases with minimal delay is difficult.

flashcards.front: What are the five ID requirements?
flashcards.back: Unique, numeric, 64-bit, ordered by date/time, and capable of generating over 10,000 IDs per second.

flashcards.front: Must IDs increase by exactly 1?
flashcards.back: No. They should increase with time, but not necessarily by exactly 1.

flashcards.front: What does time ordering mean in the requirement example?
flashcards.back: An ID created in the evening should be larger than one created in the morning on the same day.

flashcards.front: What throughput must the generator support?
flashcards.back: Over 10,000 unique IDs per second.

flashcards.front: What four designs are considered?
flashcards.back: Multi-master replication, UUID, ticket server, and Twitter Snowflake-like generation.

flashcards.front: How does multi-master replication generate unique IDs?
flashcards.back: Each database uses auto_increment with step size k, where k is the number of database servers.

flashcards.front: With two multi-master database servers, what example sequences are shown?
flashcards.back: 1,3,5,... on one server and 2,4,6,... on the other.

flashcards.front: Why can multi-master replication scale ID generation?
flashcards.back: More database servers can generate IDs in parallel using disjoint increment sequences.

flashcards.front: What are the three multi-master drawbacks?
flashcards.back: Hard across multiple data centers, IDs are not time-ordered across servers, and adding/removing servers is difficult.

flashcards.front: How large is a UUID?
flashcards.back: 128 bits.

flashcards.front: Can UUIDs be generated independently?
flashcards.back: Yes. Each web server can generate them without coordination.

flashcards.front: What synchronization advantage does UUID have?
flashcards.back: No coordination between servers is required, so the ID generators do not have synchronization issues.

flashcards.front: Why is UUID easy to scale?
flashcards.back: Each web server independently generates the IDs it consumes, so ID generation scales with web servers.

flashcards.front: Why does UUID violate the bit-length requirement?
flashcards.back: UUID is 128-bit while the design requires 64-bit IDs.

flashcards.front: Why does UUID violate the ordering requirement?
flashcards.back: UUIDs do not increase with time in the design discussed.

flashcards.front: Why does UUID violate the numeric-only requirement?
flashcards.back: UUIDs can contain non-numeric characters.

flashcards.front: What is a ticket server?
flashcards.back: A centralized database server using auto_increment to generate distributed primary-key IDs.

flashcards.front: Which company is credited with ticket servers in the chapter?
flashcards.back: Flickr.

flashcards.front: What are ticket-server advantages?
flashcards.back: Numeric IDs, easy implementation, and suitability for small- to medium-scale applications.

flashcards.front: What is the ticket server's major weakness?
flashcards.back: A single ticket server is a single point of failure.

flashcards.front: What happens if you add multiple ticket servers for availability?
flashcards.back: You introduce data-synchronization challenges.

flashcards.front: Which approach does the chapter ultimately choose?
flashcards.back: A Twitter Snowflake-like ID generator.

flashcards.front: How many total bits are in the chosen Snowflake-style ID?
flashcards.back: 64 bits.

flashcards.front: What are the five Snowflake fields?
flashcards.back: 1-bit sign, 41-bit timestamp, 5-bit datacenter ID, 5-bit machine ID, 12-bit sequence.

flashcards.front: How large is the sign field?
flashcards.back: 1 bit.

flashcards.front: What value does the sign bit use?
Why is the sign bit reserved?
flashcards.back: For future use; the chapter says it could potentially distinguish signed from unsigned numbers.

flashcards.front: How large is the timestamp field?
flashcards.back: 41 bits.

flashcards.front: What unit does the timestamp use?
flashcards.back: Milliseconds since an epoch/custom epoch.

flashcards.front: What Snowflake epoch does the chapter use?
What UTC date corresponds to that epoch?
Why are Snowflake IDs sortable by time?
flashcards.back: The 41-bit timestamp increases with time and occupies the most significant time-varying portion of the ID.

flashcards.front: How many bits are used for datacenter ID?
flashcards.back: 5 bits.

flashcards.front: How many datacenters can 5 bits represent?
How many bits are used for machine ID?
flashcards.back: 5 bits.

flashcards.front: How many machines per datacenter can 5 bits represent?
How many bits are used for the sequence number?
flashcards.back: 12 bits.

flashcards.front: How many sequence combinations are available per millisecond per machine?
When does the sequence number increment?
flashcards.back: For every additional ID generated on the same machine/process within the same millisecond.

flashcards.front: When is the sequence reset?
flashcards.back: To 0 every millisecond.

flashcards.front: When is the sequence field normally 0?
flashcards.back: Unless more than one ID is generated in the same millisecond on the same server.

flashcards.front: What is the theoretical maximum IDs per millisecond per machine?
Which Snowflake fields are generally selected at startup?
flashcards.back: Datacenter ID and machine ID.

flashcards.front: Which fields are generated while the ID generator runs?
flashcards.back: Timestamp and sequence number.

flashcards.front: Why must datacenter and machine IDs be changed carefully?
flashcards.back: Accidental changes can cause ID conflicts.

flashcards.front: What is the maximum value representable by the 41-bit timestamp?
How long does the 41-bit millisecond timestamp last?
flashcards.back: Approximately 69 years.

flashcards.front: How does a recent custom epoch help?
flashcards.back: It postpones timestamp overflow by starting the 41-bit elapsed-time count close to deployment time.

flashcards.front: What happens after the timestamp range is exhausted?
flashcards.back: A new epoch or another ID migration technique is required.

flashcards.front: What timestamp delta is shown in Figure 7-7?

flashcards.back: 1586451091225 milliseconds.

What three follow-up topics are suggested in the wrap-up?
flashcards.back: Clock synchronization, section-length tuning, and high availability.

flashcards.front: What clock assumption does Snowflake make?
flashcards.back: ID-generation servers have the same/synchronized clock.

flashcards.front: Why can clock synchronization be difficult?
flashcards.back: Clock behavior can differ across cores and machines in a distributed environment.

flashcards.front: Which synchronization technology does the chapter mention?
flashcards.back: Network Time Protocol (NTP).

flashcards.front: How can section lengths be tuned for low concurrency and long lifetime?
flashcards.back: Use fewer sequence bits and more timestamp bits.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is auto_increment difficult in a distributed ID generator?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A single database server is not large enough for the distributed target, while coordinating globally unique IDs across multiple databases with minimal delay is difficult.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare the four approaches at a high level.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Multi-master uses disjoint auto_increment sequences but has multi-data-center, time-ordering, and membership problems. UUID is decentralized and simple but 128-bit, not ordered, and potentially non-numeric. Ticket server gives easy numeric IDs but creates a central point of failure. Snowflake partitions a 64-bit ID into time, location, machine, and sequence fields and is selected because it satisfies the requirements.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is Snowflake considered divide and conquer?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Instead of trying to generate a globally unique 64-bit number as one opaque value, it divides the ID into fields that separately encode time, datacenter, machine, and same-millisecond sequence information.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain every Snowflake field.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The sign bit is one reserved bit fixed at 0; 41 timestamp bits represent milliseconds since an epoch; 5 datacenter bits identify up to 32 datacenters; 5 machine bits identify up to 32 machines per datacenter; and 12 sequence bits distinguish IDs produced by one machine in the same millisecond.

short_answer_questions.question: How does Snowflake achieve time ordering?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The 41-bit timestamp increases as time moves forward. Because this timestamp forms the major time-varying portion of the ID, IDs generated later are larger and can be sorted by creation time.

short_answer_questions.question: Why do datacenter and machine IDs matter for uniqueness?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They partition the ID-generation namespace across locations and machines. The same timestamp and sequence can therefore still produce different IDs on different configured generators.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain sequence-number behavior.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The 12-bit sequence distinguishes multiple IDs generated by the same machine in one millisecond. It increments for additional IDs and resets to zero every millisecond, giving 4096 possible values.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is the timestamp lifetime about 69 years?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A 41-bit field holds 2^41 possible millisecond positions. The maximum elapsed value is 2^41-1 = 2,199,023,255,551 ms; converting that to years yields approximately 69.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the purpose of a custom epoch?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The timestamp stores elapsed milliseconds rather than the entire absolute Unix timestamp. Choosing an epoch close to deployment makes more of the 41-bit range available for the system's future lifetime and delays overflow.

short_answer_questions.question: What follow-up risks should you discuss in an interview?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Clock synchronization across cores/machines, tuning the bit lengths for workload characteristics, and making the ID generator highly available because it is mission-critical.

practice_problems.solution: Yes. 4,096,000 theoretical IDs/second is much greater than 10,000 IDs/second.
practice_problems.note: Derived comparison from the chapter's requirement and sequence capacity.

practice_problems.prompt: Two IDs have the same timestamp, datacenter ID, and machine ID. What field must differ for both to be unique?
Two IDs have the same timestamp, machine ID, and sequence but were generated in different datacenters. What field differs?
Why can a custom epoch improve the useful lifetime of a 41-bit timestamp field?
practice_problems.solution: The field stores elapsed milliseconds since the epoch; choosing a recent epoch avoids spending bits representing time long before the system existed.

must_memorize: Requirements: unique, numeric, 64-bit, time ordered, >10,000 IDs/sec.
Traditional auto_increment does not scale cleanly across distributed databases.
Multi-master: increment by k; difficult multi-DC scaling, global time ordering, and server membership.
UUID: simple, decentralized, scalable; but 128-bit, not time ordered, potentially non-numeric.
Ticket server: easy numeric IDs; centralized single point of failure.
Layout: 1 sign + 41 timestamp + 5 datacenter + 5 machine + 12 sequence = 64 bits.
Datacenter and machine IDs are chosen at startup and should remain stable.
Timestamp makes IDs sortable by time.
Clock synchronization is an important distributed concern.
Bit sections can be tuned for workload needs.
The ID generator must be highly available.
chapter_seven_final_review.memory_chain: REQUIREMENTS -> REJECT AUTO_INCREMENT -> MULTI-MASTER -> UUID -> TICKET SERVER -> SNOWFLAKE -> 1|41|5|5|12 -> TIMESTAMP LIFETIME -> SEQUENCE THROUGHPUT -> CLOCK SYNC + BIT TUNING + HIGH AVAILABILITY
chapter_seven_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: A Snowflake-like generator creates scalable 64-bit numeric IDs by combining time, generator identity, and a per-millisecond sequence, avoiding centralized ID allocation while preserving uniqueness and time ordering.
